rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣād is an abbreviated letter and also the Qur’anic name of this sūra.
rows.anchor: The word ص is from among the abbreviated letters ( h@urūf muqat@t@a‘āt). It is also the Qur’ānic name of this sūrah.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Attempts to determine the meaning of Ṣād are needless; Islahi has discussed the abbreviated letters at the start of Baqarah’s commentary.
rows.anchor: Some people have tried to determine its meaning but in my opinion this is a needless effort.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike the Qur’an’s description as wise in Yā Sīn, this oath calls it a reminder: dhikr means reminding, and the Qur’an embodies reminders.
rows.anchor: The actual meaning of رْكِّذ is to remind. The Qur’ān is an embodiment of reminding.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an recalls truths innate to human nature that people have forgotten.
rows.anchor: It reminds man of all the truths innately found in human nature; however, he has forgotten them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an recalls divine guidance revealed through messengers for all creatures, which people had forgotten.
rows.anchor: It reminds man of the guidance which the Almighty revealed through his messengers for all His creatures and which people had forgotten.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an recalls important worldly events in which God’s mercy and punishment were manifested.
rows.anchor: It reminds man of the important incidents that took place in this world in which God’s mercy and torment manifested themselves.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an informs people of the fate that befell those who denied their messengers.
rows.anchor: It informs man of the fate met by those who denied their respective messengers.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an reminds people of their coming accountability and of reward and punishment after this world ends.
rows.anchor: It reminds man of the accountability and reward and punishment with which he will be faced once this world ends.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These aspects of the Qur’an as reminder are developed later in this sūra, especially in the cited passages.
rows.anchor: They will be further explained under verses 8-17, 46-49 and 86 of this sūrah.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath’s complement is omitted because the oath itself makes it evident; this omission suits oaths whose subject implies their complement.
rows.anchor: The complement ( muqsam ‘alayh) of this oath is not mentioned in words. It is found in the oath itself.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an’s reminders establish the truth of what the Quraysh are being told; their denial comes from ego and hostility, not doubt in the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: the reminders with which the Qur’ān is replete bear witness that what the Quraysh are being reminded of today is undeniable.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The deniers named here specifically are the Quraysh.
rows.anchor: specially refer to the Quraysh.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their rejection reflects arrogance and enmity, not any flaw in the Qur’an’s reminders; its effective reminders and sound arguments cannot sway people committed to ego and hostility.
rows.anchor: the reason for their denial is not that there is any shortcoming in the reminders of the Qur’ān; the reason is their arrogance and enmity.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning that persistent deniers will be seized by God’s punishment weighs heavily on their pride, despite the examples of earlier destroyed nations.
rows.anchor: they are being warned that if they adhere to denying the Qur’ān they will be seized by God’s punishment.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When punishment seized earlier peoples, they cried out, repented, and professed faith, but could no longer escape; repentance and faith are no longer accepted after punishment manifests.
rows.anchor: When they were seized by God, they raised a lot of hue and cry and repented and declared faith

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word talā is formed from lā with an added tāʾ; as with thumma and rabba, the added letter here specifically negates time.
rows.anchor: The word َت َلَا is actually َلَاThe letter ت is added to it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh marvel that a human being from among them was made God’s warner, and ask why the messenger was not a chief from Mecca or Ṭāʾif rather than a poor man.
rows.anchor: why was someone from among them given this status? And if at all this was to be done, why did God select a poor person for this?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The objection that a human was made messenger is addressed in verse 4; the complaint that the chosen man was poor appears in verse 8. Both express the conceit named in verse 2.
rows.anchor: This verse refers to the first of these reasons. In verse eight ahead, the second of these reasons is mentioned.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arrogance and haughtiness lead the disbelievers to call God’s messenger a sorcerer and a liar.
rows.anchor: it is because of their arrogance and haughtiness that these disbelievers regard God’s messenger to be a sorcerer and a liar.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unable to refute the Qur’an’s miraculous eloquence, the Quraysh label it sorcery to keep its effect from persuading the masses to accept it as God’s word.
rows.anchor: The Quraysh could not refute the miraculous eloquence of the Qur’ān; however, they did not want it to influence their masses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They explain the discourse’s sway as the work of a word magician rather than divine revelation, and also call the Qur’an poetry and the Prophet a poet.
rows.anchor: they would regard the Qur’ān as sorcery and the Prophet (sws) as a sorcerer.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kadhdhāb means a liar and braggart.
rows.anchor: The word ابٌ َّذَك means a person whose is a liar and a bragger.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The insult suggests that, although a word magician, Muhammad falsely claims revelation and a commission to warn; the Quraysh’s real aversion is his claim to prophethood.
rows.anchor: though this person is a magician of words but to bluff the masses he claims that whatever he says is revealed to him from God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse’s style expresses sorrow: God sent them a warner from their own people and a reminder-filled book, yet their conceit makes them mock him as sorcerer and liar.
rows.anchor: The style of this verse bears witness that it expresses sorrow at these unfortunate people.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Besides Muhammad’s prophethood, the Quraysh leaders particularly resented his call to monotheism and used it to incite their followers.
rows.anchor: the second thing which the leaders of the Quryash had great aversion to was the message of tawh@īd preached by him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because every Arab tribe blindly believed in its own god, the leaders depicted the call to one God as abolishing all other gods and as an unprecedented break with ancestral history.
rows.anchor: there are two poisonous slants hidden in this sentence: firstly, this person has done away with the all the gods except the God he believes in

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word ʿajāb conveys stronger emphasis and exaggeration than ʿajīb.
rows.anchor: has more exaggeration and emphasis in it than عََجْیبٌ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This propaganda could have incited all Arabia against the Prophet, but God protected him from its harm.
rows.anchor: this propaganda was enough to incite the whole Arabian nation against the Prophet (sws). However, the Almighty protected him against its evil.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When people were influenced by the Prophet’s monotheist message, Quraysh leaders would leave and urge others to leave too, avoid listening, and remain devoted to their deities.
rows.anchor: when at times they saw that people were being influenced by his message, they would walk away from that place

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The leaders present this as the proper course: resist the religion’s effort to make them abandon their ancestral faith and keep worshipping their gods until death.
rows.anchor: mean that this is what needs to be done.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They tell the masses that Muhammad seeks to make them forsake the religion of their ancestors, so they must cling to their gods despite his effort.
rows.anchor: the religion preached by this person is an attempt to make them renounce their ancestral religion

words: مَا سَمِعْنَا بِهَٰذَا فِى ٱلْمِلَّةِ ٱلْءَاخِرَةِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an recounts that all prophets from Noah to Abraham preached pure monotheism, while Abraham’s and Ishmael’s history and the Kaaba explain the Arabs’ true origins.
rows.anchor: all prophets of God from Noah (sws) to Abraham (sws) preached the pure message of tawh@īd.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham and Ishmael settled their descendants in Arabia to serve Islam and preach monotheism; the Kaaba was built for that purpose, but Quraysh filled it with idols.
rows.anchor: The house of God – whose custodianship is currently in the hands of Quraysh – was also built for this purpose.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’anic history struck at Quraysh’s claims and offered them no persuasive answer; stubbornly, they said their later history lacked monotheism and called the account fabricated.
rows.anchor: This history narrated by the Qur’ān was a heavy blow to the claims of the Quraysh.

words: مَا سَمِعْنَا بِهَٰذَا فِى ٱلْمِلَّةِ ٱلْءَاخِرَةِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They argue that if this account of Arab history were true, their forefathers would have transmitted some trace of it; instead, they follow and will continue their inherited religion.
rows.anchor: they have never heard the message of tawh@īd in this later part of their history

rows.speaker: Some people
rows.claim: Some identify the ‘later religion’ with the Christian nation, but Islahi rejects this for lack of contextual support; it would matter only if Quraysh believed in Christianity or Muhammad based his call on it.
rows.anchor: Some people are of the opinion that ِةَّلِمْال ِةَرِخ ْلَآا refers to the Christian nation; however, no contextual indication for this exists.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Political conceit makes the Quraysh object that, if God reveals a book to a human, he should choose a wealthy noble from Mecca or Ṭāʾif rather than Muhammad.
rows.anchor: they would say that if God wanted to reveal a book to a human being, then was He able to find only this person

words: بَلْ هُمْ فِى شَكٍّ مِّن ذِكْرِى
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their complaint about Muhammad’s selection exposes the conceit named in verse 2; they doubt the reminder because they have not yet tasted punishment and take its warning for a bluff.
rows.anchor: The verse actually expresses their arrogance referred to in verse two by the words: يِف ٍةَّزِع It is to strike at this arrogance of theirs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They are not convinced by arguments and believe only what they see; argument is being used for now, but if it fails God’s punishment will strike them.
rows.anchor: they are ones who do not get convinced from arguments and only believe in what they see.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God alone owns and distributes His treasures, including prophethood and wisdom; He may grant the highest spiritual rank to someone whom arrogant people consider low, so Quraysh cannot claim exclusive worthiness of His favours.
rows.anchor: He is the sole owner of all His treasures and also their sole distributor.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same question about possession or control of the Lord’s treasures is stated in Sūrah Ṭūr.
rows.anchor: In Sūrah T @ūr, this topic is mentioned in the following words:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If they claim dominion over the heavens and earth, let them climb to heaven and try to obstruct the mercy God is sending to His people.
rows.anchor: This verse explains what is said earlier: if they claim that the dominion of the heavens and the earth belongs to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asbāb here connotes the means or bounds associated with the heavens; the word can also mean additions and borders, discussed earlier in the commentary.
rows.anchor: This word is also used for add-ons and borders of something.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hunālika points to the place or occasion of the punishment mentioned in verse 8.
rows.anchor: The word َكِالَنُه points to the locus of the punishment referred to in verse eight

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When God’s punishment arrives, no army, however large or strong, can withstand it and it is doomed to defeat.
rows.anchor: the greatest of armies belonging to any people will not be able to stand before it; it is destined to be doomed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The noun jund is left indefinite to convey the punishment’s scope: every army, whatever its size and strength, will be routed.
rows.anchor: The word ٌندُج is not defined to express its magnitude and extent.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Companion of the pegs’ evokes tents, which are used figuratively for armies.
rows.anchor: In Arabic, pegs signify tents and from here this world is allegorically used for armies.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The figurative use resembles ‘firmly set cooking pots’ in 34:13 as an expression of Solomon’s generosity.
rows.anchor: This allegorical use of the word is similar to using the expression ٍورُدُق ٍاتَیِاسَّر to signify the generosity of a person.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The title refers to Pharaoh’s very numerous tent-dwelling armies, which drowned with him when divine punishment came; the Qur’an mentions their great number elsewhere.
rows.anchor: refers to the large number of the Pharaoh’s armies who lived in tents.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aṣḥāb al-aykah means the people of the forest, apparently named for a forest near Madyan.
rows.anchor: The expression refers to the people of Madyan. The word ُابَحْصَأُ ِةَكْیَلأَا means “forest”.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The named nations are historical proof that no faction, however powerful, survives God’s punishment: all denied messengers and were punished, as warned in verse 8.
rows.anchor: The verses under discussion provide a historical proof of this.
